source_evidence.observation: The source considers estimating the mean mu of a random variable X from independent observations X_1,...,X_N drawn from the distribution of X, and defines epsilon-accuracy as lying in the open interval (mu-epsilon, mu+epsilon).
Part (a) asks to show that sample size N = O(sigma^2/epsilon^2) suffices for an epsilon-accurate estimate with probability at least 3/4, where sigma^2 = Var X.
The proposed estimator is the sample mean mu-hat := (1/N) sum_{i=1}^N X_i.

The order notation is made explicit: there exists an absolute constant C such that N >= C sigma^2/epsilon^2 implies P{|mu-hat-mu| <= epsilon} >= 3/4; the footnote again identifies mu-hat as the sample mean.

binders: A real-valued random variable X with mean mu and variance sigma^2 (PDF page 7 / printed page 18, Exercise 2.2.9 opening and part (a)).
Independent sample variables X_1,...,X_N, each drawn from the distribution of X (PDF page 7 / printed page 18, Exercise 2.2.9 opening).
An accuracy parameter epsilon, used to form the interval (mu-epsilon, mu+epsilon) (PDF page 7 / printed page 18, Exercise 2.2.9 opening).
A positive-integer sample size N (PDF page 7 / printed page 18, Exercise 2.2.9 opening and sample-mean hint).
An absolute constant C, existentially asserted by footnote 2 and independent of X, its distribution, epsilon, and N (PDF page 7 / printed page 18, footnote 2).
hypotheses: X_1,...,X_N are drawn independently from the distribution of X (PDF page 7 / printed page 18, Exercise 2.2.9 opening).
mu is the mean of X and sigma^2 is Var X (PDF page 7 / printed page 18, Exercise 2.2.9 opening and part (a)).
N >= C sigma^2/epsilon^2 for the absolute constant C asserted by the claim (PDF page 7 / printed page 18, footnote 2).

The expressions for a finite mean and variance, and division by epsilon^2, implicitly require the relevant moments to exist and epsilon to be nonzero; the intended accuracy parameter is positive (PDF page 7 / printed page 18, Exercise 2.2.9 opening and part (a)).
conclusions: For the sample mean mu-hat = (1/N) sum_{i=1}^N X_i, the probability of epsilon-accuracy is at least 3/4 (PDF page 7 / printed page 18, Exercise 2.2.9(a), its hint, and footnote 2).
Footnote 2 states the probability conclusion explicitly as P{|mu-hat-mu| <= epsilon} >= 3/4 under the sample-size threshold (PDF page 7 / printed page 18, footnote 2).
definitions_and_conventions: mu denotes E[X], the mean being estimated (PDF page 7 / printed page 18, Exercise 2.2.9 opening).
sigma^2 denotes Var X (PDF page 7 / printed page 18, Exercise 2.2.9(a)).
mu-hat denotes the sample mean (1/N) sum_{i=1}^N X_i (PDF page 7 / printed page 18, hint and footnote 2).
The main text defines epsilon-accuracy by membership in (mu-epsilon, mu+epsilon), equivalently |mu-hat-mu| < epsilon (PDF page 7 / printed page 18, Exercise 2.2.9 opening).

The notation N = O(sigma^2/epsilon^2) is specified by footnote 2 as the existence of an absolute constant C for which N >= C sigma^2/epsilon^2 is sufficient (PDF page 7 / printed page 18, Exercise 2.2.9(a) and footnote 2).
implicit_context: The probability is taken under the joint law of the independent sample (PDF page 7 / printed page 18, Exercise 2.2.9 opening).
The constant in the O-notation is absolute rather than distribution- or parameter-dependent (PDF page 7 / printed page 18, footnote 2).
The sample-size threshold is a sufficient lower bound: every admissible integer N meeting it is covered (PDF page 7 / printed page 18, footnote 2, wording 'if N >= ... then').

details: The data are independent and identically distributed copies of X (PDF page 7 / printed page 18, Exercise 2.2.9 opening).
The estimator is a measurable function of all N observations, specifically their arithmetic mean (PDF page 7 / printed page 18, hint and footnote 2).
The requested confidence is at least 3/4 (PDF page 7 / printed page 18, Exercise 2.2.9(a)).
The body uses the strict accuracy event |mu-hat-mu| < epsilon, while footnote 2 writes the closed event |mu-hat-mu| <= epsilon (PDF page 7 / printed page 18, opening definition and footnote 2).
The sufficient scale is variance divided by squared accuracy, sigma^2/epsilon^2 (PDF page 7 / printed page 18, Exercise 2.2.9(a)).
Only existence of an absolute multiplicative constant is claimed; no optimal or numerical constant is stated (PDF page 7 / printed page 18, footnote 2).

undebatable_constraints: The estimator selected by the source is the sample mean, not an arbitrary estimator (PDF page 7 / printed page 18, hint and footnote 2).
The sample observations are independent draws from the same distribution as X (PDF page 7 / printed page 18, Exercise 2.2.9 opening).
The confidence lower bound is 3/4 (PDF page 7 / printed page 18, Exercise 2.2.9(a) and footnote 2).
The sample-size dependence is proportional, up to an absolute constant, to sigma^2/epsilon^2 (PDF page 7 / printed page 18, Exercise 2.2.9(a) and footnote 2).
The absolute constant must not depend on the distribution of X or on the parameters of the particular instance (PDF page 7 / printed page 18, footnote 2, phrase 'absolute constant').
The probability guarantee is conditional on meeting the lower bound N >= C sigma^2/epsilon^2 (PDF page 7 / printed page 18, footnote 2).

ambiguities.issue: The exercise's opening definition uses an open accuracy interval, whereas footnote 2 formulates the event with <= epsilon.
ambiguities.evidence: PDF page 7 / printed page 18: the opening says '(mu-epsilon, mu+epsilon)', while footnote 2 writes P{|mu-hat-mu| <= epsilon} >= 3/4.
ambiguities.impact: At distributions having positive probability exactly at error epsilon, the strict and non-strict success events can differ; a formal target must choose or explicitly relate these boundary conventions.

ambiguities.issue: No numerical value or optimality assertion for the absolute constant C is given.
ambiguities.evidence: PDF page 7 / printed page 18, footnote 2: it says only 'there exists an absolute constant C'.
ambiguities.impact: Any fixed universal constant that proves the stated implication can realize the source claim, but the source does not require a particular constant.

ambiguities.issue: Integer rounding and a positive minimum sample size are not written explicitly in the asymptotic expression.
ambiguities.evidence: PDF page 7 / printed page 18, Exercise 2.2.9(a) and footnote 2: N is a sample size and is compared directly with the real quantity C sigma^2/epsilon^2, without a ceiling or max-with-one convention.
ambiguities.impact: A formal statement must encode N as an integer and ensure the sample mean's division by N is meaningful, especially when sigma^2 is zero or the real-valued threshold is below one.

ambiguities.issue: Moment-existence and positivity assumptions are used but not separately enumerated.
ambiguities.evidence: PDF page 7 / printed page 18, Exercise 2.2.9: the text refers to mu, Var X, epsilon-accuracy, and sigma^2/epsilon^2 without a formal assumption list.
ambiguities.impact: A formalization must state enough integrability or square-integrability and epsilon > 0 to define the quantities and justify the bound; these are inherited mathematical well-formedness conditions rather than an additional substantive restriction.

contract_plain_english: Exercise 2.2.9(a) says that for independent observations X_1,...,X_N distributed like a real random variable X with mean mu and variance sigma^2, the sample mean mu-hat estimates mu to accuracy epsilon with probability at least 3/4 once N is at least an absolute constant times sigma^2/epsilon^2. The main definition uses strict error |mu-hat-mu| < epsilon, while the explanatory footnote writes |mu-hat-mu| <= epsilon; the source gives no particular value of the universal constant (PDF page 7 / printed page 18, Exercise 2.2.9(a), hint, and footnote 2).
